objections.claim: The amendment amended AROUND the regression rule and lost the rule. Turn-1's operative sentence — 'a qualified measurement may not regress >10% against the previous qualified release without an expiring waiver carrying product + release sign-off' — no longer appears anywhere in the amended entry. Clause 6 now states the rule's DOMAIN (clauses 1-4 only) and BASE CASE (activates from the second qualified release) and the waiver form, but the rule itself survives only as the name 'the ±10% rule'. Adopting these bytes adopts a regression regime whose operative text does not exist in the adopted record; a future reader must reconstruct the bound, its direction, and its modal force from a nickname. Worse, the nickname changes the semantics: '±10%' denotes deviation in EITHER direction, while turn-1's text bound regressions only — on the bytes as written it is arguable that a >10% IMPROVEMENT breaches the rule, which is absurd and therefore exactly the kind of textual defect this corpus's bytes-over-prose discipline exists to kill. This is the report-ahead-of-bytes failure class in a new costume: the amendment narrates the rule's properties while the rule itself fell out of the bytes.

objections.proposedFix: Restore one operative sentence at the head of clause 6: 'A qualified clause 1-4 measurement may not regress more than 10% against the previous qualified release without a waiver in the register's full form.' Strike '±' (the rule binds regressions, not improvements) or, if a symmetric investigation trigger on large improvements is actually intended, decide that expressly — never by a glyph.

objections.claim: The named macOS runner class underdetermines one of the four slice platforms. 'Base-configuration Apple Silicon entry chip (M1-class), 8 GB' is the reference for BOTH macOS arm64 and macOS x86_64 — but an M1-class machine executes x86_64 binaries only under Rosetta 2 translation, which has a materially different cold-start profile (first-run translation cost, translation cache state interacting with the gate's cold-cache protocol) than native Intel hardware. Whether the macOS x86_64 numbers mean 'native Intel class' or 'Rosetta-on-M1' is a CLASS question, not a machine-identifier/OS/cache PINNING question — so as written it falls outside what the entry delegates to the harness-naming act, and the harness-namer would co-author the threshold's meaning for that platform: precisely the hazard MF-2's amendment closed for the other three. The fix is one clause; either resolution is defensible (Intel hardware is scarce in CI fleets; Rosetta-on-M1 is arguably the representative environment for remaining x86_64 macOS users), but the entry must choose.
objections.evidence: docs/coop/COORDINATOR-DECISIONS.md lines 714-721 (runner-class bullet: one macOS class, no x86_64 provision) against the Scope bullet's four platforms (line 700: 'macOS arm64/x86_64, Linux x86_64/arm64'); the pinning delegation names 'EXACT machine identifiers, OS versions and cache-state protocol' — class selection for x86_64-on-macOS is none of those.
objections.proposedFix: Add one clause to the runner-class bullet, e.g.: 'macOS x86_64 binds to the same M1-class hardware under Rosetta 2, translation state recorded in the harness's cache-state protocol' — or name a native Intel class instead. Either way the class decision is made HERE; the harness-naming act pins, it does not choose.

objections.claim: The DR-115 fate bullet coins a status label the register does not have: '`DECIDED-V1-NOT-INTEGRATED`-analog form'. The register's status vocabulary is closed (HARD-BLOCKED / OPEN / PROPOSED-CLOSED-FOR-REVIEW / DECIDED-V1-NOT-INTEGRATED / SATISFIED), and DECIDED-V1-NOT-INTEGRATED's own definition — 'product authority decided the posture, while the required accepted successor remains missing' — fits DR-115's decided-not-measured state exactly, so no analog is needed. Under the D-001 MF-6 discipline, register-content changes (which a new status label would be) are DECISIONS, not hygiene.
